_link.title: I can describe the attractive and repulsive interactions between magnetic poles, and compare these to electric and gravitational interactions

toLevel2.question: What happens when two magnetic north poles are brought close together?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Like magnetic poles (north–north or south–south) always repel each other.

distractors.answer: They attract each other
distractors.explanation: Only unlike poles (north and south) attract; like poles repel.

distractors.answer: They have no interaction
distractors.explanation: Two magnets always interact; like poles push apart.

distractors.answer: They cancel each other out
distractors.explanation: Magnetic poles do not cancel; like poles repel.

toLevel2.question: Which pair of magnetic poles will attract each other?
toLevel2.correct: A north pole and a south pole
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Unlike magnetic poles attract each other.

distractors.answer: A north pole and a north pole
distractors.explanation: Two north poles are like poles, so they repel.

distractors.answer: A south pole and a south pole
distractors.explanation: Two south poles are like poles, so they repel.

distractors.answer: Two isolated magnetic monopoles
distractors.explanation: Magnetic monopoles have never been observed; magnets always have both poles.

toLevel2.question: Which type of fundamental interaction can only attract and never repel?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Gravity only attracts; there is no gravitational repulsion between masses.

distractors.answer: Magnetic interaction
distractors.explanation: Magnetic poles can both attract (unlike poles) and repel (like poles).

distractors.answer: Electrical interaction
distractors.explanation: Electric charges can both attract (unlike charges) and repel (like charges).

distractors.answer: All three interactions
distractors.explanation: Only gravity is purely attractive; magnetic and electric interactions can also repel.

toLevel2.question: How do the interactions between electric charges compare to those between magnetic poles?
toLevel2.correct: Both can attract and repel depending on the type of charge or pole
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Unlike charges attract and like charges repel, just as unlike poles attract and like poles repel.

distractors.answer: Electric charges only attract, while magnetic poles attract and repel
distractors.explanation: Electric charges can also repel; like charges push each other away.

distractors.answer: Electric charges only repel, while magnetic poles only attract each other
distractors.explanation: Both electric charges and magnetic poles can attract and repel.

distractors.answer: Electric charges have no interaction, unlike magnetic poles that repel
distractors.explanation: Electric charges interact strongly; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

toLevel2.question: What happens when a north pole of one magnet faces the south pole of another magnet?
toLevel2.correct: The two magnets pull toward each other
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Unlike poles (north and south) attract, pulling the magnets together.

distractors.answer: The two magnets push away from each other
distractors.explanation: Only like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

distractors.answer: The two magnets rotate to face the same way
distractors.explanation: The magnets attract each other directly; they do not simply rotate.

distractors.answer: The two magnets have no effect on each other
distractors.explanation: Unlike poles always attract; they do not ignore each other.

toLevel2.question: Two south magnetic poles brought close together will repel each other.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Like poles repel, so two south poles push each other apart.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Students may confuse like and unlike pole interactions; like poles always repel.

toLevel2.question: Gravitational interactions between two masses can be either attractive or repulsive.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Gravity is always attractive. Unlike magnetism and electricity, there is no gravitational repulsion.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Students may assume gravity works like magnetism and electricity, but gravity only attracts.

toLevel2.question: Unlike magnetic poles {{blank:1}} each other, while like magnetic poles {{blank:2}} each other.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A north pole and a south pole attract; two north poles or two south poles repel.

blank:1.explanation: Unlike poles attract, not repel; like poles repel.
Magnetic poles interact with forces; they do not cancel each other.

blank:2.explanation: Like poles repel, not attract; unlike poles attract.
Like poles always interact; they repel each other.

toLevel2.question: Gravity can only {{blank:1}}, whereas magnetism and electricity can both attract and {{blank:2}}.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Gravitational interactions are always attractive. Magnetic and electric interactions can be attractive or repulsive.

blank:1.explanation: Gravity always attracts; there is no gravitational repulsion.
Gravity is a force of attraction between masses, not a form of radiation.

blank:2.explanation: The correct term for pushing apart is repel, not cancel.
Repel is the correct term for like charges or like poles pushing apart.

toLevel2.question: A north pole and a south pole are {{blank:1}} poles, so they {{blank:2}} each other.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: North and south are different (unlike) poles, and unlike poles attract.

blank:1.explanation: North and south are different types of pole, so they are unlike, not like.
Magnetic poles are always north or south; they are not neutral.

blank:2.explanation: Unlike poles attract each other; like poles repel.
Unlike poles always interact; they attract each other.

toLevel3.question: Why does gravity differ fundamentally from magnetic and electric interactions?
toLevel3.correct: Gravity has only one type of source (mass), so it can only attract
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Mass is always positive, so gravitational interactions are always attractive. Magnetism has two pole types and electricity has two charge types, allowing both attraction and repulsion.

distractors.answer: Gravity has two types of source (mass), so it can attract and repel
distractors.explanation: Mass comes in only one form; there is no negative mass, so gravity cannot repel.

distractors.answer: Gravity is stronger than magnetism, which prevents any repulsion
distractors.explanation: The strength of gravity does not determine whether it can repel; the absence of a second source type does.

distractors.answer: Gravity only acts on very large objects, so repulsion is not noticeable
distractors.explanation: Gravity acts on all masses regardless of size; the lack of repulsion is due to having only one source type.

toLevel3.question: Two bar magnets are placed with their north poles facing each other. How does this compare to bringing two positive charges together?
toLevel3.correct: Both interactions are repulsive, because like sources repel
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Like magnetic poles repel just as like electric charges repel. In both cases, identical source types push apart.

distractors.answer: Both interactions are attractive, because similar sources attract
distractors.explanation: Like sources repel in both magnetism and electricity; they do not attract.

distractors.answer: The magnetic interaction is repulsive but the electric one is attractive
distractors.explanation: Both like poles and like charges repel; the pattern is the same.

distractors.answer: The magnetic interaction is attractive but the electric one is repulsive
distractors.explanation: Like poles repel just as like charges repel; neither is attractive.

toLevel3.question: Which statement correctly compares gravitational and magnetic interactions?
toLevel3.correct: Gravitational interactions are always attractive; magnetic interactions can be attractive or repulsive
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Gravity only attracts because mass has no opposite type. Magnetism can attract (unlike poles) or repel (like poles).

distractors.answer: Both gravitational and magnetic interactions are always attractive between objects
distractors.explanation: Magnetic interactions can be repulsive when like poles face each other.

distractors.answer: Gravitational interactions can repel; magnetic interactions always attract each other
distractors.explanation: Gravity never repels, and magnetism can repel when like poles interact.

distractors.answer: Both gravitational and magnetic interactions can attract or repel depending on type
distractors.explanation: Only magnetism and electricity can both attract and repel; gravity can only attract.

toLevel3.question: A student says: 'Magnetic and electric interactions follow the same attract–repel pattern.' Is this correct?
toLevel3.correct: Yes — unlike sources attract and like sources repel in both interactions
toLevel3.correctExplanation: In both magnetism and electricity, unlike types (poles or charges) attract and like types repel.

distractors.answer: No — magnetic poles only attract, while electric charges attract and repel
distractors.explanation: Magnetic poles can also repel when like poles face each other.

distractors.answer: No — electric charges only attract, while magnetic poles attract and repel
distractors.explanation: Electric charges can also repel when like charges are near each other.

distractors.answer: No — both interactions are always attractive regardless of source types
distractors.explanation: Both magnetic and electric interactions can be repulsive between like sources.

toLevel3.question: What makes magnetism and electricity similar when comparing their interactions?
toLevel3.correct: Both involve two types of source that can attract or repel each other
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Magnetism has north and south poles; electricity has positive and negative charges. Unlike types attract and like types repel.

distractors.answer: Both involve one type of source that can only attract other objects
distractors.explanation: That describes gravity. Magnetism and electricity each have two source types.

distractors.answer: Both involve sources that always repel and never attract each other
distractors.explanation: Both can attract (unlike sources) as well as repel (like sources).

distractors.answer: Both are identical to gravity in their attract-repel behaviour pattern
distractors.explanation: Gravity only attracts; magnetism and electricity can both attract and repel.

toLevel3.question: Two masses are brought near each other. What interaction occurs between them?
toLevel3.correct: They attract each other regardless of their composition
toLevel3.correctExplanation: All masses attract each other gravitationally. Unlike magnetism and electricity, there is no repulsive gravitational interaction.

distractors.answer: They repel each other if they are the same material
distractors.explanation: Gravity does not depend on material type; all masses attract.

distractors.answer: They attract only if the masses are of different sizes
distractors.explanation: All masses attract regardless of their relative sizes.

distractors.answer: They have no interaction until they are in direct contact
distractors.explanation: Gravity acts over any distance between masses, not only on contact.

toLevel3.question: Electric charges follow the same attract–repel pattern as magnetic poles: unlike types attract and like types repel.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Both magnetic poles and electric charges exhibit attraction between unlike types and repulsion between like types.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Students may think only one of these interactions can repel, but both follow the same pattern.

toLevel3.question: Magnetism and electricity each have {{blank:1}} types of source, while gravity has only {{blank:2}} type of source.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Magnetism has north and south poles; electricity has positive and negative charges. Gravity has only mass, which is always positive.

blank:1.explanation: Magnetism has two types (north and south); electricity has two types (positive and negative).
Both magnetism and electricity have exactly two types of source, not three.

blank:2.explanation: Gravity has only one type of source (mass); there is no negative mass.
Gravity has one type of source (mass); saying zero would mean gravity has no source.

toLevel3.question: Like magnetic poles {{blank:1}} each other, which is similar to how like electric charges {{blank:2}} each other.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Both like poles and like charges experience a repulsive force, pushing them apart.

blank:1.explanation: Like poles repel; only unlike poles attract.
Like poles push apart; they do not neutralise each other.

blank:2.explanation: Like charges repel; only unlike charges attract.
Like charges push apart; they do not neutralise each other.

toLevel3.question: Gravity is unique among the three interactions because it can only {{blank:1}}, never {{blank:2}}.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Gravity is always attractive between any two masses. There is no gravitational repulsion.

blank:1.explanation: Gravity always attracts; it never repels.
Gravity is an attractive force, not a form of radiation.

blank:2.explanation: Gravity always attracts; it is repulsion that gravity cannot do.
The correct contrast is that gravity cannot repel.

toLevel4.question: A student sets up two bar magnets on a frictionless surface with their south poles facing each other. What will be observed?
toLevel4.correct: The magnets will accelerate away from each other
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Like poles (south–south) repel, so on a frictionless surface the magnets accelerate apart.

distractors.answer: The magnets will accelerate toward each other
distractors.explanation: Like poles repel, not attract; the magnets push apart.

distractors.answer: The magnets will remain completely stationary
distractors.explanation: Like poles exert a repulsive force, causing acceleration on a frictionless surface.

distractors.answer: The magnets will spin in circles around each other
distractors.explanation: The repulsive force pushes the magnets directly apart along the line between them.

toLevel4.question: A north pole is placed near a south pole of another magnet, and separately two positive charges are brought together. Which combination of interactions occurs?
toLevel4.correct: The poles attract each other and the charges repel each other
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Unlike poles attract, while like charges repel. These follow the same pattern: unlike sources attract, like sources repel.

distractors.answer: Both the poles and the charges attract each other simultaneously
distractors.explanation: The unlike poles attract, but like charges repel; they do not both attract.

distractors.answer: Both the poles and the charges repel each other simultaneously
distractors.explanation: Unlike poles attract; only the like charges repel.

distractors.answer: The poles repel each other and the charges attract each other
distractors.explanation: Unlike poles attract (not repel) and like charges repel (not attract).

toLevel4.question: An astronaut releases two steel balls in space far from any planet. What interaction occurs between them?
toLevel4.correct: They attract each other gravitationally and drift together slowly
toLevel4.correctExplanation: All masses attract gravitationally. In space with no friction, the balls will slowly accelerate toward each other.

distractors.answer: They repel each other and drift apart through empty space
distractors.explanation: Gravity only attracts; there is no gravitational repulsion between masses.

distractors.answer: They remain motionless because there is no gravity in space
distractors.explanation: Gravity exists everywhere between masses; the balls attract each other even in space.

distractors.answer: They orbit each other only if one ball is much larger in size
distractors.explanation: Any two masses attract gravitationally regardless of relative size.

toLevel4.question: A student argues that since like poles repel, like masses should also repel. What is wrong with this reasoning?
toLevel4.correct: Mass only comes in one form, so gravity can only attract and never repel
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Unlike magnetism, there is no 'negative mass.' All mass is positive, so gravitational interactions are always attractive.

distractors.answer: Like masses do repel, but the force is too weak to detect easily
distractors.explanation: Gravity between masses is always attractive; there is no repulsive component regardless of strength.

distractors.answer: Masses must be charged before they can repel each other at all
distractors.explanation: Gravitational repulsion does not exist; charging creates electric repulsion, not gravitational.

distractors.answer: Masses repel only at very short distances below one millimetre apart
distractors.explanation: Gravity is attractive at all distances; there is no transition to repulsion.

toLevel4.question: Which scenario demonstrates a repulsive interaction?
toLevel4.correct: Two north magnetic poles placed near each other on a table
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Like magnetic poles repel each other, pushing the magnets apart.

distractors.answer: A ball falling toward the surface of the Earth from a height
distractors.explanation: This is gravitational attraction, not repulsion.

distractors.answer: A north pole placed near a south pole of another bar magnet
distractors.explanation: Unlike poles attract; this is an attractive interaction.

distractors.answer: Two heavy objects moving toward each other due to their mass
distractors.explanation: Masses attract gravitationally; this is attraction, not repulsion.

toLevel4.question: How would you classify the interaction between a negative charge and a positive charge?
toLevel4.correct: Attractive, because unlike charges attract each other
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Just as unlike magnetic poles attract, unlike electric charges attract each other.

distractors.answer: Repulsive, because opposite charges push apart from each other
distractors.explanation: Unlike (opposite) charges attract, not repel.

distractors.answer: Neutral, because the charges cancel each other out completely
distractors.explanation: The charges interact with an attractive force; they do not simply cancel.

distractors.answer: Gravitational, because all particles interact via gravity first
distractors.explanation: The dominant interaction between charges is electrical, not gravitational.

toLevel4.question: A student creates a table comparing interactions. Which row is correct?
toLevel4.correct: Gravity: attract only | Magnetism: attract and repel | Electricity: attract and repel
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Gravity is purely attractive. Both magnetism and electricity can attract (unlike sources) and repel (like sources).

distractors.answer: Gravity: attract and repel | Magnetism: attract only | Electricity: attract and repel
distractors.explanation: Gravity only attracts; magnetism can both attract and repel.

distractors.answer: Gravity: attract only | Magnetism: attract only | Electricity: attract and repel
distractors.explanation: Magnetism can both attract and repel, not just attract.

distractors.answer: Gravity: attract and repel | Magnetism: attract and repel | Electricity: attract only
distractors.explanation: Gravity only attracts, and electricity can both attract and repel.

toLevel4.question: When two south poles face each other they {{blank:1}}, but when a north pole faces a south pole they {{blank:2}}.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Like poles (south–south) repel, while unlike poles (north–south) attract.

blank:1.explanation: Like poles repel; only unlike poles attract.
Two south poles push apart; they do not cancel.

blank:2.explanation: Unlike poles attract; only like poles repel.
Unlike poles pull together; they do not cancel.

toLevel4.question: Electric and magnetic interactions can both attract and repel, but {{blank:1}} interactions can only {{blank:2}}.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Gravity is unique because it is always attractive — there is no gravitational repulsion.

blank:1.explanation: Magnetic interactions can both attract and repel; gravity is the one that only attracts.
Electric interactions can both attract and repel; gravity is the one that only attracts.

blank:2.explanation: Gravity only attracts; it never repels.
Gravity is an attractive force between masses, not radiation.

toLevel4.question: Two positive charges {{blank:1}} each other, which is analogous to two north magnetic poles that also {{blank:2}} each other.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Like charges repel and like poles repel — the pattern is the same for both interactions.

blank:1.explanation: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
Like charges push apart; they do not neutralise.

blank:2.explanation: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
Like poles push apart; they do not neutralise.

toLevel5.question: If a hypothetical 'negative mass' existed, how would gravitational interactions change compared to the current model?
toLevel5.correct: Gravity could repel as well as attract, similar to magnetic and electric interactions
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Currently gravity only attracts because mass is always positive. A second type of mass would allow repulsion, paralleling magnetism and electricity.

distractors.answer: Gravity would still only attract, because the force law requires positive values
distractors.explanation: The attractive-only nature of gravity arises from one mass type; a second type would enable repulsion.

distractors.answer: Gravity would become a contact force and cease to act at a distance entirely
distractors.explanation: Introducing negative mass would not change gravity from a field interaction to a contact force.

distractors.answer: Gravity would become identical to magnetism in all measurable aspects observed
distractors.explanation: Even with negative mass, gravity would differ from magnetism in many properties like source type and field geometry.

toLevel5.question: Why is the absence of magnetic monopoles significant when comparing magnetic interactions to electric interactions?
toLevel5.correct: Both still show attract–repel behaviour, but magnetic sources are always dipoles while electric charges can exist alone
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Electric charges can be isolated (a single proton), but magnets always have both a north and south pole. Despite this, both interactions follow the same attract–repel pattern.

distractors.answer: It means magnetism can only attract while electricity can attract and repel between charges
distractors.explanation: Magnetism can both attract and repel between poles, even though monopoles do not exist.

distractors.answer: It proves that magnetic interactions are a special case of gravitational force between objects
distractors.explanation: Magnetism is fundamentally different from gravity; the absence of monopoles does not link them.

distractors.answer: It shows that magnetic poles cannot interact at all without being broken into monopoles first
distractors.explanation: Magnetic poles interact via their dipole fields without needing to be separated into monopoles.

toLevel5.question: A student claims: 'Since electric and magnetic interactions follow the same attract–repel pattern, they must be the same force.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.correct: The claim is incorrect; they share the same pattern but differ in source type and field structure
toLevel5.correctExplanation: While both follow like-repels and unlike-attracts, magnetism arises from poles (always in pairs) and electricity from isolated charges. They are related but distinct.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct; both are the same force expressed in different experimental setups
distractors.explanation: Although related through electromagnetism, they are distinct interactions with different sources.

distractors.answer: The claim is incorrect; electric interactions only attract and never repel between charges
distractors.explanation: Electric interactions can both attract and repel; that is not the reason the claim is wrong.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct; all three fundamental interactions are identical at the atomic scale
distractors.explanation: Gravity, electricity, and magnetism are distinct interactions with different properties.

toLevel5.question: Why can you use the same 'like repels, unlike attracts' rule for both magnetic poles and electric charges?
toLevel5.correct: Both interactions involve two opposite types of source that create symmetric attractive and repulsive forces
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Magnetism has north/south poles and electricity has positive/negative charges — two-type systems that produce the same interaction pattern.

distractors.answer: Because both interactions are caused by gravity acting on charged particles at distance
distractors.explanation: Gravity is a separate interaction; it does not cause magnetic or electric forces.

distractors.answer: Because all forces in nature follow identical patterns regardless of their different sources
distractors.explanation: Not all forces follow this pattern; gravity, for example, only attracts.

distractors.answer: Because magnetic poles and electric charges are physically the same type of particle present
distractors.explanation: Magnetic poles arise from current loops or atomic dipoles; they are not the same as electric charges.

toLevel5.question: Consider a universe where gravity could both attract and repel. Which existing interaction would it most closely resemble in behaviour?
toLevel5.correct: It would resemble electric or magnetic interactions, with two source types enabling both outcomes
toLevel5.correctExplanation: If gravity had two mass types, its interaction pattern would mirror the attract–repel behaviour seen in magnetism and electricity.

distractors.answer: It would still be unique because gravity acts on mass rather than on charges or poles
distractors.explanation: While the source differs, the attract–repel pattern would make the behaviour analogous to electricity and magnetism.

distractors.answer: It would not resemble any known interaction because repulsive gravity is theoretically impossible
distractors.explanation: The question asks about a hypothetical scenario; the behaviour would match existing two-source interactions.

distractors.answer: It would be identical to friction because friction also pushes objects apart on surfaces
distractors.explanation: Friction is a contact force, not a field interaction; it does not follow the attract–repel pattern.

toLevel5.question: A student observes that two magnets repel and two identically charged spheres also repel. They conclude that gravity must also repel identical objects. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
toLevel5.correct: The student incorrectly assumes all field interactions have two source types; gravity has only one
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Magnetism and electricity have two source types allowing repulsion, but gravity has only mass (one type), so it can only attract.

distractors.answer: The student is correct; identical masses do repel but the force is too small to measure
distractors.explanation: Gravity between masses is always attractive regardless of measurement precision.

distractors.answer: The flaw is that magnets and charges do not actually repel in real experimental conditions
distractors.explanation: Like poles and like charges do repel; the flaw is in extending this pattern to gravity.

distractors.answer: The student forgot that gravitational repulsion only occurs at distances beyond one kilometre
distractors.explanation: Gravitational repulsion does not occur at any distance; gravity is always attractive.

toLevel5.question: Rank gravity, magnetism, and electricity by the number of distinct source types each interaction involves, from fewest to most.
toLevel5.correct: Gravity (one) has the fewest, then magnetism (two) and electricity (two) are equal
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Gravity has one source type (mass). Magnetism has two (north and south poles). Electricity has two (positive and negative charges).

distractors.answer: Electricity (one) has the fewest, then gravity (two), then magnetism has three types
distractors.explanation: Electricity has two charge types; gravity has one mass type; magnetism has two pole types.

distractors.answer: All three have the same number of source types with exactly two distinct sources each
distractors.explanation: Gravity has only one source type (mass); it does not have a second opposite type.

distractors.answer: Magnetism (one) has the fewest, then electricity (two), then gravity has three source types
distractors.explanation: Magnetism has two pole types; gravity has only one; none have three.

toLevel5.question: Why is comparing magnetic, electric, and gravitational interactions a key part of the VCE Physics study design?
toLevel5.correct: It reveals how the number of source types determines whether an interaction can be attractive only or also repulsive
toLevel5.correctExplanation: This comparison shows that having two source types (poles or charges) enables repulsion, while having one type (mass) restricts the interaction to attraction only.

distractors.answer: It proves that all three interactions are mathematically identical with the same equations used
distractors.explanation: While all three use inverse-square laws, their source types and behaviours differ fundamentally.

distractors.answer: It shows that gravitational interactions are always stronger than magnetic or electric interactions
distractors.explanation: Gravity is actually the weakest of the three at particle scales; the comparison focuses on interaction patterns.

distractors.answer: It demonstrates that magnetic interactions are irrelevant compared to the other two interaction types
distractors.explanation: Magnetism is essential in physics; the comparison highlights its similarities and differences with the others.

toLevel5.question: The fact that gravity has {{blank:1}} source type means it can only attract, whereas magnetism and electricity each have {{blank:2}} source types, allowing both attraction and repulsion.
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Mass is the single source of gravity (always positive). Magnetism has north/south poles and electricity has positive/negative charges — two types each.

blank:1.explanation: Gravity has only one source type (mass); there is no 'negative mass.'
Gravity has one source type (mass); zero would mean no source exists.

blank:2.explanation: Both magnetism and electricity have two source types, enabling both attraction and repulsion.
Both magnetism and electricity have exactly two source types, not three.

toLevel5.question: Although magnetic poles always exist as {{blank:1}}, electric charges can exist as isolated {{blank:2}}, which is a key difference between these two interactions.
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Magnets always have both a north and south pole (dipole), but a single positive or negative charge (monopole) can exist on its own.

blank:1.explanation: Magnetic monopoles have never been observed; magnets are always dipoles.
Bar magnets are dipoles with two poles, not quadrupoles.

blank:2.explanation: Individual charges are monopoles; a dipole involves two opposite charges separated.
A single charge is a monopole, not a quadrupole.
